html:
The Santo Niño de Cebú is a small wooden statue of the Child Jesus, given by Ferdinand Magellan in 1521 to the ruler of Cebu and his wife at their Christian baptism. It is the oldest Christian object in the Philippines and the symbol of its Catholic faith.

Magellan's Spanish fleet, sailing west around the world, reached the Philippines in March 1521. At Cebu the ruler, Rajah Humabon, agreed to be baptised with his wife and hundreds of his people, and received the statue. Weeks later Magellan was killed at the Battle of Mactan fighting the chief Lapulapu, and the survivors left. Humabon's Christianity did not last.

In 1565 the expedition of Miguel López de Legazpi came to Cebu to found a Spanish colony. After a fight, a soldier found the statue in a burned house, unharmed. The Spanish took this as a miracle and built a church on the spot, now the Basílica del Santo Niño.

From there Spanish rule and Catholic missions spread across the islands, part of European colonial rule in Southeast Asia. Today the Philippines has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world. The statue is the only canonically crowned image of Jesus in the country, and every January hundreds of thousands come to Cebu for the Sinulog festival in its honour.
